case.title_in_the_review_set: 58-year-old man with hypertensive pulmonary edema: norepinephrine in a congested, pump-limited patient

human_evidence.faculty_interpretation_as_reported:
The pressure rise itself is physiologically understandable.

However:

the patient is already profoundly hypertensive with acute cardiogenic pulmonary edema.

Norepinephrine is clinically inappropriate and drives pressure further into an extreme range.

IMPORTANT:

This REJECT is primarily a judgment of the MANAGEMENT CONTEXT / EDUCATIONAL USE of this intervention.

It is NOT, by itself, evidence that the common vascular-tone mechanism requires global recalibration.

Do NOT retune T merely to make norepinephrine look acceptable in a patient who should not receive it.
human_evidence.the_reject_is_not_converted: the REJECT stays a REJECT of the management action; it is not a mechanism failure and it is not softened into an acceptance

intervention.as_reviewed: Norepinephrine 10 mcg/min, started at minute 5 and kept at that rate to the end. Nothing else is given or changed; the underlying problem is left untreated.

is_not: a change of the case's physiology
an educational claim about pump-limited families
purpose: To show that a physiologically understandable pressor response can still be a clinically inappropriate management action: the response of the common mechanism is what it is, and the order is the wrong one for this patient. Physiologic response is not appropriate management.
titration_and_stop: not part of this scenario: it is the single start the faculty reviewed; nothing in it was re-run with a rate change

use.future: a management-reasoning scenario in which the order is available and its consequence can be judged; building it is a separate decision

what_it_is_evidence_of: a pressure response in the expected direction and with a plausible timing (Q1 Expected, Q2 Plausible)
a management action the faculty rejected for this patient (Q3 Too large, Q4 Incoherent, Q5 Yes: already profoundly hypertensive, acute cardiogenic pulmonary edema)
